claims.text: Classical molecular dynamics simulations can be used to study the size-dependent thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a strong size-dependent thermal response.
Approximately 2 nm-radius FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles begin atomic rearrangement at lower temperatures than approximately 10 nm-radius particles.
Approximately 2 nm-radius FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles melt at lower temperatures than approximately 10 nm-radius particles.
The lower transition temperatures of smaller nanoparticles arise from their enhanced surface-to-volume effects.
As-synthesized FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a randomized high-entropy atomic distribution.
A heating ramp from approximately 300 K to 1200 K at rates of 10^10–10^12 K/s is suitable for comparing FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles of different sizes.
An NVT ensemble with fixed volume properly represents nanoparticle surface effects during these simulations.
Nanoparticle size and its associated surface-to-volume ratio influence atomic mobility.
Nanoparticle size and its associated surface-to-volume ratio influence surface energy.
Nanoparticle size and its associated surface-to-volume ratio influence phase transitions.
Heating promotes atomic diffusion in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Heating promotes surface instability in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The higher proportion of surface atoms in smaller nanoparticles causes disordering at lower temperatures.
The higher proportion of surface atoms in smaller nanoparticles causes melting at lower temperatures.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles exhibit faster onset of atomic diffusion than larger nanoparticles under identical heating conditions.
Potential choice and molecular-dynamics timescale affect the estimated transition temperatures.
Differences between molecular-dynamics and experimental heating rates can cause discrepancies when extrapolating simulation results to experiments.
